abstract: Sleep spindles, 9-16 Hz transient oscillatory bursts in the sleep electroencephalogram (EEG), are linked to memory consolidation and are altered in aging and disease states. Recent work suggests that traditionally detected spindles are only a subset of a larger class of spindle-like events, and that beyond spindles exist several classes of spindle-like transient oscillatory activity. Together these classes have been shown to comprise individualized signatures of brain activity linked to disease states including schizophrenia and REM behavior disorder. While traditional spindle activity has been studied across the lifespan, the evolution of the full set of spindle-like oscillation classes as a function of age is unknown. To address this major knowledge gap, we characterize the cross-sectional dynamics of multiple classes of spindle-like oscillations in whole-night polysomnography from the Cleveland Family Study (n = 704, age: 7-89 y). Unsupervised clustering revealed five classes of spindle-like events in the delta (2-4 Hz), theta (4-6 Hz), theta-alpha (6-9 Hz), sigma-low (9-12 Hz) and sigma-high (12-16 Hz) ranges, each with separate, stereotyped cross-sectional dynamics across the lifespan. Large heterogeneity was observed even within narrow classically defined demographics. Early life ([~]10-25 years) is marked by parallel age-related increases in the frequency of the sigma-high and theta-alpha classes and a rapid shift of fast-spindle coupling toward the slow-oscillation peak -- timing thought to be critical for memory consolidation. Midlife ([~]25-50 years) marks the maximal expression of the delta and sigma-low classes together with an increasingly central-dominant distribution of fast spindles. Late life is defined by progressive uncoupling of lower frequency events from the slow oscillation as well as a leftward shift of higher frequency events away from the peak of the slow oscillation. We further uncover a developmental axis in which slow-oscillation phase coupling decreases in frequency dependence with age. Moreover, we show that the combination of expressed event classes can define phenotypes whose prevalence shifts systematically with age. Together, these provide a robust multi-modal framework for characterizing lifespan dynamics, with wide applications spanning both mechanistic and clinical studies.
